blocks.text: **The problem.** Given the `root` of a binary search tree and two integers `low` and `high`, return the **sum of every value in the range [low, high]**, inclusive.

blocks.alt: The tree 10, 5, 15, 3, 7, null, 18 with low 7 and high 15. The values in range are 7, 10 and 15, which sum to 32. Node 3 is too small, so its left subtree can be skipped; 18 is too big, so its right subtree can be skipped.

blocks.text: The idea: prune what can't be in range

Summing every node works for any tree. A BST lets you skip whole subtrees: if a node is **below `low`**, everything on its left is smaller still — only its **right** side can contain values in range. If it's **above `high`**, only its **left** side can. Only nodes inside the range need both sides searched.
**Time O(n), space O(h).** Ignores the ordering.

blocks.caption: Too small: only the right side can help. Too big: only the left. In range: add it and search both sides.

blocks.text: **Time O(h + k)** where k is the number of values in range — the walk only enters a subtree that can hold an answer. **Space O(h).** In the worst case (everything in range) it's still O(n), but a narrow range in a big balanced tree costs about O(log n).
3. The same pruning with a stack
**Time O(h + k), space O(h)** for the stack — the same work without recursion.

blocks.alt: Visit every node: O(n) time, O(h) space. Pruned recursion: O(h + k) time, O(h) space. Pruned stack: O(h + k) time, O(h) space.

items: **Everything in range** — every node is visited; no pruning helps.
**low = high** — at most one value counts.
**Range covers the root only** — both children may still need checking.
**Count nodes in a range** — the same pruning, adding 1 instead of the value.
**All values in a range, sorted** — an in-order walk with the same pruning.
**Trim a BST** — keep only the nodes in range, re-linking the rest (Pattern 2).
